Modeling is an important aspect of synthetic biology, where scientists and
researchers test and engineer the viable aspect of their final product prior to
stepping foot into a laboratory. Our modelling workflow primarily deals with the
reengineering of the BtSULT enzyme for 5 steroid specificity.
Enzyme Engineering
Wild type(WT) BtSULT is a sulfotransferase derived from Bacteroides
thetaiotamicron that solubilizes steroid molecules such as DHEA. BtSULT was
selected after its biochemical characterization by Yao et. al (2022), demonstrating
sulfotransferase activity on bile acids. However, the substrate selectivity profile of
BtSULT reveals its inability to accept 5 steroid molecules due to a flat A/B
fusion ring, such as 5 -LCA. This fact necessitates an engineering process to
redesign the WT BtSULT active site to sulfonate 5 -LCA for PCS treatment
BtSULT was selected as the main engineering scaffold instead of its mammalian
homolog, SULT2A1, considering BL21 expression bottlenecks. SULT2A1 crystal
structures were utilized from UniProt as a structural template for active-site
redesign.
The ideal reaction mechanism that indicates a working BtSULT mutant for wet-lab
validation prioritizes sulfur-group transfer from PAPS to LCA 3-OH for production
of sulfolithocholic acid, or sulfo-LCA.
According to Kakuta et. al (1998), their study of human estrogen sulfotransferase
activity asserts sulfuryl transfer is only possible if the catalytic base contacts the
substrate OH at hydrogen bond range, 2.7 to 3.1 Å. This is to be considered in our
engineering process.

1. Structural Study of BtSULT
Although human SULT2A1 is well-studied and documented, BtSULT is not,
requiring a study to identify candidates for a proposed catalytic base. Our early
studies assumed BtSULT used histidine as a catalytic base, similar to His99 in
human SULT2A1 (PDB: 1J99). Clustal Omega homology alignment tentatively
suggested His215 as the closest histidine (Fig. 1). Extrapolating from the
conserved PAPS binding motif, we also elect E136 as a catalytic base candidate.
However, homology alignments were later disproved to be completely viable,
partly due to the 15.2% sequence identity according to a Foldseek structural
alignment (see below).

Round 0 of mutagenesis screening for the proposed enzyme prioritized a
6x-alanine scan, geared towards validating expression bottlenecks in-vitro prior to
the final variant being reengineered. Steric clashes were changed to alanine as a
proxy for catalytic activity in order to prioritize enzyme binding energy. This work
was done prior to further structural studies, where Boltz-2 structural distances and
review of literature confirmed the presence of mediating residues such as lysine,
tyrosine, and glutamate as a divergent catalytic base to histidine in human
AK1RD1. The mutations are as follows: E144A, W161A, K211A, F248A, F249A,
T252A
3.1 Point Mutation Panel
The first technique draws from our structural studies by introducing point
mutations into the active site of BtSULT. The proposed catalytic base of E144 was
mutated to aspartate due to its similar yet shorter sidechain, with hopes to relieve a
steric clash. Additionally, F147 was mutated to serine as a nonfunctional sidechain,
testing if F147 was a selectivity marker for 5β steroids as it was in human carbonic
anhydrases (Brynda et al.).
In order to finalize F147’s mutation to serine, a saturation mutagenesis study was
conducted, prioritizing transfer distance between the substrate and PAPS and base
distance as a proxy for bond formation after mutating F147. The results are
displayed in Table 3.

lines.text: Serine prioritized the lowest transfer distance and had the smallest base distance,
suggesting the formation of an h-bond, now acting as a stabilizing residue to
position the substrate more tightly into the catalytic pocket (Fig. 4).
The first round of point mutations specifically searched for a switch between
DHEA, the native substrate, and LCA selectivity in WT and mutated BtSULT.
Such was done by mutating, in addition to mutations E144D and F147S, two PAPS
motif residues R236 and T252 into R236K and T252S, probing the PAPS side
geometry with a shorter reach and introducing a charge conserving residue,
respectfully. His215 from then on was disproved as a catalytic base and mutations
F147S seemed to decrease specificity for DHEA when the WT catalytic base was
above the measured 2.91 Å OH distance in PDB 3F3Y .

Additionally, a 3X alanine background was added to each variant, following clash

SULT2A1 loop 3 was split into its three functional segments for candidate design:
its substrate binding region, the loop’s hinge region, and the PAPS binding motif.
These three segments were interchanged across 10 variants along two segments of
BtSULT plus additional flanking residues. Residues 153-190 hosted a BtSULT
specific insertion, revealed by the initial ClustalOmega alignment and its proximity
to the proposed E144 catalytic region. The substrate-binding region of SULT2A1
was grafted to this region. The C-terminus of BtSULT, aligning with SULT2A1’s
catalytic loop, hosted either a grafted substrate-binding motif, a PAPS-binding
motif, or both (Fig. 7).
Additionally, a 3X alanine background was added to each variant, following clash
analysis of the 6X alanine background from Round 0 and Round 1. Glu144 and
Lys211 had been assigned as key pocket residues and were therefore not mutated.
Similarly, Trp161 was left unchanged due to its location in the 153-190 BtSULT
insertion. This controlled our analysis of variants with grafts in the 153-190 region
instead of adding a confounding variable (Fig. 8).
